w: Home of Liverpool FC since 1892, originally used by Everton from 1884 before their move to Goodison Park. Seats 61,276 across four stands including the famous Kop end. Record attendance of 61,905 was set in 1952 against Wolverhampton Wanderers, and capacity grew after 2024 redevelopment.

Everton's home from 1892 until the club's 2025 move to Hill Dickinson Stadium, after which Everton Women took over the ground. Hosted the 1910 FA Cup Final and matches at the 1966 World Cup. Located in Walton, two miles north of Liverpool city centre, with an all-seated capacity of 39,414.

Home of Bundesliga side Hamburger SV since 1953, with a capacity of 57,000 making it Germany's eighth-largest stadium. Hosted matches at the 2006 FIFA World Cup and UEFA Euro 2024, and briefly served as FC Shakhtar Donetsk's continental home during the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
_facts: Hosted Shakhtar Donetsk during the war

w: Known since 2021 as the Polsat Plus Arena Gdansk, this 41,620-seat stadium in the Letnica district opened in 2011 and is home to Lechia Gdansk. It hosted four UEFA Euro 2012 matches, including a quarter-final, and the first international there ended 2-2 between Poland and Germany in 2011.

Home of Red Star Belgrade since 1963 and known as Marakana, this Dedinje ground seats 51,755 spectators. Renamed in 2014 for club legend Rajko Mitic, it hosted the 1973 European Cup final and the 1976 UEFA European Championship finals, the highest-capacity stadium in Serbia today.
_facts: Home of Red Star Belgrade since 1963

w: Home ground of Olympiacos in Piraeus, named after War of Independence hero Georgios Karaiskakis who was mortally wounded nearby. Capacity of 33,334 makes it Greece's largest football-specific stadium. Hosted the 2023 UEFA Super Cup after the original Kazan venue was ruled out over Russia's UEFA suspension.

Home of FC Zurich and Grasshopper Club Zurich, and the athletics club LC Zurich, originally built in 1925 and rebuilt in 2007. Hosts the annual Weltklasse Zurich Diamond League meet since 1928. On its track on 21 June 1960, Armin Hary became the first man to run 100 metres in 10.0 seconds.
s: FC Zurich's home, Weltklasse athletics venue
_facts: Home of FC Zurich and Grasshopper Club

w: Home of Sheffield Wednesday since opening in 1899, with a capacity of 34,835 across four covered stands. Site of the Hillsborough disaster on 15 April 1989, when 97 Liverpool fans died at an FA Cup semi-final, prompting the Taylor Report's stadium safety reforms including all-seater requirements.

Designed by architect Torben Grut and opened in 1912 as the main venue for that year's Olympic Games, hosting athletics, football, wrestling, gymnastics and tug of war. Known locally simply as Stadion, it holds 13,145 to 14,500 depending on configuration, or nearly 33,000 for concerts.
s: 1912 Olympics main stadium, still in use

w: Home of Sporting CP in Lisbon, built beside the site of the club's earlier ground of the same name. The stadium honors Jose Alvalade, who founded Sporting Clube de Portugal in the early 20th century and was its first club member, with a listed capacity of over 52,000.
s: Sporting CP's home, named for its founder
_facts: Built beside the club's earlier stadium

w: Indoor arena on the Greenwich Peninsula, opened in its present form in 2007 within the shell of the former Millennium Dome. Ranks third among UK indoor venues by seating capacity, behind Co-op Live and Manchester Arena, and was the world's busiest music arena in 2008. Nearest station is North Greenwich.
s: Greenwich Peninsula arena inside the old Dome
_facts: Third-largest UK indoor venue by capacity

w: Home of La Liga side Real Sociedad since it opened in 1993 in San Sebastian's Basque Country. Capacity was restored to 40,000 after a 2019 redevelopment, up from a reduced 26,800, making it the 11th-largest stadium in Spain. It is a proposed host venue for the 2030 World Cup.

Multi-purpose Gothenburg stadium built for the 1958 FIFA World Cup, seating 43,000 with a 75,000 concert capacity. Hosted the UEFA Euro 1992 final, two UEFA Cup finals, and world speed skating and athletics championships, and stages the yearly opening ceremony of the Gothia Cup youth tournament.

Built for the 1908 Summer Olympics and demolished in 1985, this west London venue hosted the marathon finish, swimming, boxing and a 1966 World Cup match. From 1927 it staged greyhound racing, running the English Greyhound Derby until closing in 1984. The site is now occupied by White City Place.

Former 15,276-seat football stadium in Barcelona, sited across from Camp Nou, where it served Barcelona B, the women's team and Juvenil A. Replaced by the newly built Estadi Johan Cruyff, it was demolished after that stadium's completion on 27 August 2019.
s: Barcelona B's former ground by Camp Nou
_facts: Home of Barcelona B and women's team
Replaced by Estadi Johan Cruyff in 2019

w: Norway's best-known international sports arena, host to 15 speed skating world records and more than 50 track and field world records. The original stadium was demolished in 2004 and replaced by the current New Bislett Stadium, completed in 2005 and designed by C.F. Moller Architects.
_facts: 15 speed skating world records set here

w: Small football stadium in the capital of Andorra, built in 1990 with a capacity of 1,249 and its own running track. Together with the Camp d'Esports d'Aixovall it hosted Andorra's top two football divisions, and staged all Andorra national team games until the Estadi Nacional opened in 2014.

Indoor arena in Turin's Olympic Park, built for the 2006 Winter Olympics at a cost of 87 million euros to host ice hockey. Opened in December 2005 with a basketball capacity of 16,600, it is Italy's largest indoor sporting arena and has hosted the ATP Finals tennis tournament since 2021.
s: 2006 Olympics arena, ATP Finals host since 2021
_facts: Built for 2006 Winter Olympics ice hockey

w: Home of AC Sparta Prague, this Prague stadium regularly also hosts the Czech Republic national football team's home matches. Its official seating capacity stands at 18,887, making it one of the country's principal football venues.

Home of Legia Warsaw since 9 August 1930, located in the Powisle area of Warsaw's Srodmiescie district. Rebuilt in two stages between 2008 and 2011, with space for 31,103 spectators it ranks as the 5th-biggest stadium in Ekstraklasa. Long owned by the Polish Armed Forces, it now belongs to the City of Warsaw.

Home of Barcelona Femeni, Barcelona B and the Juvenil A youth team, located at the club's Ciutat Esportiva training complex in Sant Joan Despi, about 7 km from Camp Nou. Named for Johan Cruyff after his 2016 death, this UEFA Category 3 venue holds 6,000 and replaced the demolished Mini Estadi.
_facts: Home of Barcelona B and Femeni

w: Home of SK Rapid Wien in Vienna's Hutteldorf district, built on the site of the former Gerhard Hanappi Stadium. For international matches it carries the sponsor-free name Weststadion. The venue opened with a Rapid friendly against Chelsea on 16 July 2016, followed a week later by its first competitive match.
_facts: Built on former Gerhard Hanappi Stadium site

w: Multi-purpose indoor arena in Budapest named after Hungarian boxer Laszlo Papp, Hungary's second-biggest sports complex after the MVM Dome. Holds up to 12,500 for concerts, 11,390 for boxing and 9,479 for ice hockey. Built to replace the Budapest Sports Hall, destroyed by fire in December 1999.
s: Budapest arena named for boxer Laszlo Papp
_facts: Capacity 9,479 for ice hockey, 12,500 for concerts
Replaced Budapest Sports Hall after 1999 fire

w: Former home of Grasshopper Club Zurich in the city's Kreis 5 district, opened in 1929 with room for 27,500 and hosting matches at the 1954 FIFA World Cup. Capacity grew to 38,000 by 1986 before shrinking to 17,666 by its 2007 closure, after which Grasshoppers moved to the Letzigrund.

Home ground of FC Lugano in Lugano, Switzerland, with a capacity of 6,330 used mainly for football matches. The stadium hosted one match during the 1954 FIFA World Cup. A 2008 plan by Lugano's political authorities to renovate it for Swiss Super League requirements was announced but never carried out.
s: FC Lugano's home, 1954 World Cup venue

w: Multi-purpose stadium in the El Menzah district of Tunis, built in 1967 on the site of the former Velodrome Stadium to host that year's Mediterranean Games. It has served the city ever since as a major venue, with a listed capacity of 39,858 spectators.
s: Tunis venue built for the 1967 Med Games
_facts: Built on former Velodrome Stadium site

w: Indoor arena in Madrid's Casa de Campo fairgrounds, minutes from the city centre, built on the site of the old Rocodromo climbing wall. Designed in 2001 by Spanish firm Estudio Cano Lasso as a venue for sporting, commercial, cultural and leisure events; also known as Telefonica Arena under a sponsorship deal.
_facts: Located in Casa de Campo fairgrounds

w: Equestrian stadium in Chamonix, France, that hosted the opening and closing ceremonies of the 1924 Winter Olympics, the first Winter Games. Also staged cross-country skiing, curling, figure skating, ice hockey, military patrol and speed skating events during that inaugural tournament. It holds 45,000.
s: Venue for the first-ever Winter Olympics, 1924
_facts: Also staged ice hockey and figure skating in 1924

w: Indoor multi-purpose arena in Sarajevo used for various events at the 1984 Winter Olympics and later as the main venue of the 2019 European Youth Olympic Winter Festival. Renamed in 2010 in honour of Juan Antonio Samaranch after his death, though still widely known as Zetra Olympic Hall.
_facts: Renamed for Juan Antonio Samaranch in 2010
Main venue of 2019 European Youth Olympic Winter Festival

w: Home of Korona Kielce in Poland, built in 2006 and known for sponsorship reasons as EXBUD Arena. It seats 15,500 and opened on 1 April 2006 with an Ekstraklasa match against Zaglebie Lubin that finished 1-1. The club's old stadium is now used by the reserve team, Korona Kielce II.

Indoor arena in Turin, also called the Oval Olympic Arena, built specifically for the 2006 Winter Olympics to host the speed skating competitions. It has a listed capacity of 8,500 spectators and remains a legacy venue of that Games.
_facts: Also known as Oval Olympic Arena

w: Stadium in Tomblaine near Nancy, France, built in 1926 and used by Ligue 2 club Nancy. Completely rebuilt and reinaugurated in 2003, it now holds 20,087 people. Since summer 2010 it has been one of the few French stadiums fitted with artificial turf.

Home of Tranmere Rovers since opening in 1912, formerly also used by Liverpool Reserves and Liverpool Women. Rebuilt in 1995 to meet Taylor Report all-seater rules, it now holds 16,587 across four stands including the Kop. Its record crowd of 24,424 came for a 1972 FA Cup tie against Stoke City.

Football stadium in the Hisingen area of Gothenburg, Sweden, previously known as Bravida Arena and as Hisingen Arena for UEFA competitions. Initiated by Allsvenskan side BK Hacken together with Gothenburg Municipality to provide a purpose-built venue seating 6,000 to 7,000 spectators.
_facts: Linked to Allsvenskan side BK Hacken
Known as Hisingen Arena in UEFA play

w: Multi-purpose stadium in the Bologhine district of Algiers, Algeria, serving mainly as the home ground of USM Alger for football matches. The venue is generally used for league fixtures and has a listed capacity of 10,000 spectators.
s: USM Alger's home ground in Bologhine

w: Former home of Bolton Wanderers from 1895 to 1997, hosting the 1901 FA Cup final replay. Site of one of English football's worst disasters in 1946, it was later immortalised in L.S. Lowry's 1953 painting Going to the Match. The stadium was demolished in 1999, two years after Bolton moved to the Reebok Stadium.
_facts: Depicted in L.S. Lowry's Going to the Match

w: Multi-purpose sports venue in Dublin's Ballsbridge suburb, owned by the Royal Dublin Society since 1879 and home to the Dublin Horse Show since 1881. Primary tenant Leinster Rugby plays United Rugby Championship and Champions Cup games here. Capacity is 18,500, expandable past 40,000 for concerts.
_facts: Hosts the Dublin Horse Show since 1881
Owned by the Royal Dublin Society

w: Multi-purpose stadium in the Mohamed Belouizdad district of Algiers, Algeria, serving as the home ground of CR Belouizdad football club. The venue is used mainly for league matches and has a listed capacity of 15,000 spectators, one of the capital's principal football grounds.
s: CR Belouizdad's home ground in Algiers
_facts: Located in Mohamed Belouizdad district, Algiers

w: Multi-purpose stadium on the Hohe Warte hill in Heiligenstadt, part of Vienna's 19th district of Dobling. Primarily a football venue, it is home to First Vienna FC and has also hosted Austrian international rugby union matches and the Vienna Vikings American football team.
_facts: Home of Vienna Vikings American football
